analysis.one_liner: Bars states from collecting income or wealth taxes from anyone who moves out of the state.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or a House floor vote and died at the end of the 117th Congress in January 2023, with no Democratic cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would stop any state, city, or other taxing jurisdiction from making a former resident pay its income tax or wealth tax after that person permanently moves somewhere else. States like New York and California tax people who are residents, and some states have debated ways to keep taxing people who leave; this bill would shut all of that down nationwide. The people with the most to gain are high earners in high-tax states who can afford to relocate — for example, moving to Florida or Texas and wiping out their old state's claim on their income. The cost falls on state budgets: the money not collected from wealthy leavers would have to be made up by the remaining residents through higher taxes or cuts to schools, roads, and services.
analysis.who_benefits: Wealthy and high-income residents of high-tax states who move to lower-tax states would gain the most: the bill would end their former state's ability to collect income tax or wealth tax from them after they relocate. Because the bill defines "similar tax" broadly to cover taxes on income, assets, or net wealth, it would shield relocating households from a wide range of state and local tax claims, not just专门 exit taxes. Middle-income movers would also be covered, but they generally have smaller tax bills to escape and often already pay little or no tax to the state they left.

how_it_helps.text: For anyone who relocates, the bill would bar their former state — and every local government in it — from imposing any obligation to collect income tax, wealth tax, or a similar tax on assets or annual income.
It would have applied to calendar years starting after December 31, 2021, and covered every level of government from states down to cities, counties, and special taxing districts.

analysis.who_pays: State and local governments would lose revenue they could have collected from people who leave, and ordinary residents would bear the difference through higher taxes, cuts to services, or both. The bill also raises the odds of disputes over where someone "really" lives, since the old state would have no way to enforce a tax claim once a person claims to have moved.

drawbacks.text: The bill would have shrunk state and local revenue by letting high earners end their income tax obligations to a state simply by relocating, meaning either higher taxes on remaining residents or cuts to schools, roads, and other services everyone uses.

It applied to income taxes, not just exit-specific taxes, and left it to the person's new state to define when someone counts as a 'resident' and is no longer a resident of the old state — making it easier to formally relocate on paper while keeping substantial ties to the original state.

Supporters would argue the bill prevents double taxation of genuinely mobile workers who move but keep working for an employer in their old state; the cost an honest supporter must acknowledge is that the same rule lets the wealthiest households legally detach from the tax systems of the states whose services they spent years using.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's stated appeal is real but narrow: a few people genuinely get taxed twice by a state they left, and a clean rule against that has some fairness. But the bill as written was far broader than that problem: it would have barred any state from collecting income or wealth taxes from anyone claiming to have moved, on top of already-existing constitutional limits, and states had no way to challenge dubious moves. The main predictable effect was to let high earners in high-tax states opt out of the tax systems that fund schools, roads, and services they used, with the bill made up through higher taxes or cuts for everyone else. Weighing a modest anti-double-taxation benefit against a large, one-sided transfer to the wealthy, the costs clearly outweigh the benefits for ordinary people.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and later to a subcommittee, but no committee or floor vote was ever scheduled before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. David Schweikert introduced the Exit Tax Prevention Act on March 23, 2021, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day.
On October 19, 2021, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Antitrust, Commercial, and Administrative Law — a step that set it aside rather than advancing it.
Seven Republicans cosponsored the bill; no Democrats joined.
No further action was taken, and the bill expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State governments and their remaining taxpayers are better off: the rule that would have let wealthy residents end their income tax obligations by relocating never came close to law, so no revenue hole opened in state budgets.

for.name: Reps. Scott Perry, Tracey Mann, C. Scott Franklin, Jody Hice and 3 other Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all seven cosponsors were Republicans.

against.name: Rep. Jerrold Nadler
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee the bill was assigned to; the bill sat through referral and subcommittee referral without ever receiving a markup or vote.

sides.party_line_note: All eight sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans and no Democrat signed on; the bill also died quietly in a committee chaired by a Democrat, so the fight was less a vote than a lack of movement.

industries.note: The bill would let wealthy residents of states like New York or California end their income and wealth tax obligations to that state by relocating, regardless of the taxes that financed the services they used. The savings concentrate at the top, while the lost revenue is made up by everyone else.

States would lose the power to enforce income and wealth tax obligations against people who claim to have moved out, weakening their main revenue tool. The gap would likely be filled by higher taxes or service cuts affecting all remaining residents.
